title: Will Venezuela announce a presidential election before 2027?
resolution_criteria: This question resolves as **Yes** if, before January 1, 2027, Venezuela officially announces a new presidential election. In order to count, the announcement must be made by a person or entity with the legal authority to do so, the announcement must name a specific election date, and voting must be scheduled to take place before January 1, 2028.
background:
Since [the US capture of Nicolás Maduro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_intervention_in_Venezuela) in January 2026 and Delcy Rodríguez's subsequent interim Venezuelean presidency there has been speculation as to when the next presidential election will be held.

On August 27, 2026, [the Venezuelan National Assembly unanimously approved](https://elpais.com/america/2026-08-27/la-asamblea-venezolana-acelera-la-reforma-del-supremo-promovida-por-estados-unidos.html), in its first reading, a [partial reform of the Supreme Court of Justice (TSJ) Law](https://elpais.com/america/2026-08-13/el-chavismo-y-la-oposicion-venezolana-acuerdan-renovar-a-todos-los-magistrados-del-supremo.html "https://elpais.com/america/2026-08-13/el-chavismo-y-la-oposicion-venezolana-acuerdan-renovar-a-todos-los-magistrados-del-supremo.html"). This legislative step is part of the ongoing political dialogue agreements between the Venezuelan government and opposition, under the support and guidance of the US government. This process aims to form a new high court, a step the opposition considers essential for restoring the country's institutions and establishing an electoral roadmap.

In early September 2026, [Rodríguez stated ](https://www.cubaheadlines.com/articles/339452)her nation would hold elections when "ready," without providing a specific timeline. [US President Trump agreed with this](https://www.turkiyetoday.com/world/trump-says-venezuela-not-ready-yet-for-elections-3227329).

On September 14, [a new coalition](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/opposition-group-calls-for-presidential-election-in-venezuela-with-maria-corina-machado-as-candidate/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX09XRUZWQzcwMDE2MTI5OTIwMDE), called Alianza por Venezuela, consisting of nine political and social organizations, called for "free, fair and verifiable" presidential elections, with Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado to serve as its candidate.

comments.author: DeRuina
comments.text: I think the key thing to watch here is not whether Venezuela commits to elections, but whether the CNE names a specific presidential date, since that is what resolves this. The US plan, as reported by Axios on Sep 23, runs TSJ reform, then a new CNE, then a date. The TSJ law only passed on Sep 1 and magistrates still have to be chosen, so a new CNE seated before December looks tight. Reuters (Sep 25) also cited sources saying a voter-roll update could take up to a year, pushing any vote toward late 2027 or beyond. The trap I see is the December CNE calendar: it has to cover regional and municipal races anyway, so a headline about "elections announced" could easily be sub-national only. On the other side, that same December announcement is the most plausible YES path — bundling a 2027 presidential date into it would be a cheap way to satisfy Rubio's "months, not years" framing. Has anyone seen a concrete timeline for when the National Assembly expects to seat the new CNE?

comments.author: Theomachado
comments.text: I started at a 7% chance based on my research. After talking to a couple of Venezuelan friends, they told me that even though markets are pricing it in at about 10%, the change is at most 1%, and sentiment in the country is that it won't happen before 2027. With this primary source information I backed my forecast to about 3% 😂.

comments.author: DaiLothbrook
comments.text: I started with a 6% base rate for an announcement during the roughly 100 days remaining in 2026. I moved down because recent reporting indicates that a vote is unlikely before the end of 2027 and describes several unresolved institutional prerequisites, including changes to the electoral council, courts and voter rolls. The government has publicly promised eventual elections but has avoided giving a date. Since announcing an election is easier than actually holding one, I retain a small chance of a surprise decree. My current estimate is 3.5%, with a plausible range of 2%–6%.

comments.author: Koboh
comments.text:
<u>**My forecast: 8%.**</u>

* I’m putting this below 30% mainly because the latest evidence points to a fairly slow transition. Delcy Rodríguez has publicly committed to elections, which keeps the probability meaningfully above zero, but there is still no announced timetable. More importantly, Reuters reported on September 25 that several political sources and analysts expect the vote could be delayed by a year or more because of planned reforms to the courts and electoral authorities. 

[https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/venezuelas-promised-elections-face-long-delays-sources-say-2026-09-25/](https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/venezuelas-promised-elections-face-long-delays-sources-say-2026-09-25/)

* The timing matters here. Chatham House noted earlier this year that Venezuela’s constitution requires an election to be announced at least six months before it is held, while a credible process would also require reforms to the CNE, electoral rules, voter registration, and dispute-resolution mechanisms.

[https://www.chathamhouse.org/2026/04/democratic-elections-venezuela-wont-happen-overnight-heres-groundwork-thats-needed-first-4](https://www.chathamhouse.org/2026/04/democratic-elections-venezuela-wont-happen-overnight-heres-groundwork-thats-needed-first-4)



So I wouldn’t interpret “**elections are coming” as strong evidence for a 2026 announcement.** The more useful signals would be a formal electoral timetable, concrete CNE reforms, agreement with opposition actors, or the start of an official election-preparation process.



* I am keeping 8% rather than going much lower because the political process is clearly moving toward an eventual election, and Rodríguez has now made the commitment publicly. But there is a big difference between committing to elections in principle and actually setting the machinery in motion.



<u>***My estimate: 8% YES / 92% NO.***</u> ***Rodríguez’s commitment matters, but without a formal timetable or concrete election preparations, I’m still heavily leaning toward no announcement before 2027.***

comments.author: craber
comments.text:
It was reported by Reuters as of recently that Venezuela's promised elections face long delays. Due to planned "overhauls" of courts and electoral systems despite the "promise of a transition to a full democracy" by acting President Delcy Rodriguez. Given the requirements made by the US for a 'democracy' in Venezuela must be accompanied by [economic and ‌social stability](https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/trump-venezuelas-rodriguez-discuss-debt-restructuring-rubio-says-2026-09-23/)", the current "administration is currently prioritizing economic stability and oil-related" implementations over the focus of sovereignty and elections in Venezuela. As reported by the Guardian after the Department of War secured US majority control of oil reserves in Venezuela. The US state department said “it’s not a deal with the interim government of Venezuela and there was not a political process included in the negotiations”, despite the official claim by the US president that "the United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela."

Thus, given the circumstances, I would place the likelihood of Venezuela announcing a presidential election before 2027 as very low given the economic interest and influence from the US, plus the current economic and political instability of Venezuela. Which would have to overhaul their electoral system before successfully transitioning from years of authoritarian rule into a functioning democracy.

comments.author: lubossaloky
Bas_
comments.text: Some opposition parties have come out against the oil deal that the US made recently (which involves a large amount of oil going to the US and a Venezuelan oligarch for free). They have also claimed that any agreements made by the current regime are invalid and that only a democratically chosen government can speak for the country. This means that a democratic government might scrap or modify oil deals that have been made, which might make the US hesitate before pushing for elections. Oil opportunities have been cited by US officials as one of the main motivators of the regime change in Venzuela, and they are also crucial to getting the economy back on track (which is probably a precondition for establishing a stable democracy)
